title: AI Made Me Look Foolish. Then I Learned
gist: Astrophysicist Paul M. Sutter describes rebuilding his decade-old VIDE void-finding algorithm with AI coding agents at his elbow — 10x faster, handling surveys 100x larger, with the agents also generating plots and drafting commentary — and flags that the agents never once hesitated when he checked their reasoning. The free portion cuts off at a membership wall before the failure is described.

insights.claim: AI coding agents rewrote the core of a decade-old scientific algorithm faster than its original author could and without the typos, producing a version 10 times faster that handles surveys a hundred times larger.
insights.speaker: Paul M. Sutter
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude scientific-software speedups from agentic coding are now first-person reported by domain experts, not vendor benchmarks — the productivity claim has real evidence behind it.
insights.quote: Coding agents rewrote the core of the algorithm, faster than I could have and without the typos.
insights.locator: I had spent weeks on it

insights.claim: The agents' contribution extended past code into generating the plots and drafting the commentary for the write-up, meaning AI now touches the full research output chain rather than just implementation.
insights.speaker: Paul M. Sutter
insights.so_what: If figures and interpretive text are agent-generated, the error surface of published science shifts from coding bugs to unreviewed reasoning — a systemic risk for research-dependent industries.
insights.quote: When it came time to write it up, they generated the plots and drafted the commentary that went with them.
insights.locator: I had spent weeks on it

insights.claim: The improvement Sutter valued most was not raw speed but the agents' handling of real-world data pathologies — the gaps, masks, and ragged boundaries absent from textbook versions of the problem.
insights.speaker: Paul M. Sutter
insights.so_what: Messy-data edge-case handling, historically the most expensive human engineering time, is where agents deliver the most value — the right place to look for adoption in scientific and industrial software.
insights.quote: the gaps and masks and ragged boundaries that never show up in the textbook version of the problem
insights.locator: Best of all, it had a far more sophisticated way

themes.theme: Unhesitating confidence as the failure mode

insights.claim: Every time the author checked the AI agents' reasoning, they never once hesitated — uniform confidence with no calibrated uncertainty signal is the setup for the embarrassment the piece describes.
insights.speaker: Paul M. Sutter
insights.so_what: Absence of a hesitation signal removes the natural human check on delegated work; tools that expose calibrated uncertainty are the missing layer in agentic workflows.
insights.quote: Every time I checked their reasoning, they never once hesitated.
insights.locator: I had spent weeks on it

insights.claim: The author frames ancient alchemy as the right historical analogue for understanding chatbots — a practice that produced real technique alongside confident error.
insights.speaker: Paul M. Sutter
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for pricing AI capability: genuine capability and systematic delusion coexisting in the same practice rather than one replacing the other.
insights.quote: Ancient alchemy has a lot to teach us about chatbots
insights.locator: AI Made Me Look Foolish dek

insights.claim: A working scientist publicly describes AI as indispensable to weeks of specialist algorithm work while simultaneously reporting it made him look foolish, indicating adoption is running ahead of verification practice in academic research.
insights.speaker: Paul M. Sutter
insights.so_what: The gap between agent adoption and verification tooling is an open product opportunity and a reproducibility risk to watch in published research.
insights.quote: I had also spent those weeks with an AI at my elbow, and it had been indispensable.
insights.locator: I had spent weeks on it
